title: Ndolé
ingredients: 500g ndolé leaves (bitterleaf, fresh or dried, deveined and washed to reduce bitterness)
1 scotch bonnet pepper, whole (optional, for heat)
instructions: Boil the ndolé leaves in water for 15 minutes, then drain, rinse, and squeeze out excess water to reduce bitterness; repeat rinsing once more and finely chop the leaves.
In a large pot, boil the beef chunks with chopped onion, garlic, stock cubes, and salt until tender, about 40 minutes, reserving the cooking liquid.
Add the smoked fish to the beef pot and simmer for 10 minutes to let the flavors combine.
Stir the ground roasted peanuts into a little warm water to form a smooth paste, then add it into the pot along with the palm oil.
Add the chopped ndolé leaves and shrimp to the pot, along with the whole scotch bonnet pepper if using.
Simmer uncovered over low heat for 30-40 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens and the oil rises slightly to the top.
Adjust salt to taste, remove the whole pepper, and serve hot with boiled plantains, rice, or fufu.

title: Achu Soup (Yellow Soup)
ingredients: 2 tbsp limestone/kanwa (potash), dissolved in a little water
300g cow skin (kanda), cleaned and cut into pieces
1 tsp African nutmeg (njangsa), ground (optional, traditional flavoring)
instructions: Boil the cocoyams in water until very soft, about 30-40 minutes, then drain and pound them in a mortar (or mash thoroughly) until smooth and stretchy; keep warm.
In a separate pot, boil the beef and cow skin with a stock cube and salt until tender, reserving the cooking broth.
In a clean pot, heat the palm oil gently and stir in the dissolved potash water; the oil will turn a bright yellow color as you whisk.
Add the reserved meat broth gradually to the yellow oil, whisking continuously to form a smooth, slightly thickened yellow sauce.
Stir in the ground crayfish, smoked fish, cooked beef, cow skin, and remaining stock cube, and simmer for 10 minutes.
Season with salt and njangsa if using, and adjust the consistency with a little more broth if too thick.
Mold the pounded cocoyam into a smooth dome on a serving plate and ladle the hot yellow soup over or beside it.
Serve immediately while both the achu and soup are hot.

title: Koki (Bean Pudding)
ingredients: 1 scotch bonnet pepper, chopped (adjust to taste)
Banana leaves (or plantain leaves), cleaned and softened over flame
instructions: Soak the black-eyed peas for a few hours, then rub off and rinse away the skins until the beans are clean and pale.
Blend or grind the peeled beans with the onion, scotch bonnet pepper, and a small amount of water into a thick, smooth batter.
Pour the batter into a large bowl and whisk in the palm oil, ground crayfish, stock cube, and salt until well combined and slightly fluffy.
Cut the softened banana leaves into portions and fold each into a cone or pouch shape, spooning in the bean batter and folding the leaf closed securely.
Arrange the wrapped parcels in a large pot with a little water at the bottom, and steam over medium heat for about 1.5 to 2 hours, topping up water as needed.
Check that a parcel is firm and set in the center before removing all from heat.
Let cool slightly before unwrapping, and serve warm as a side or light meal.

title: Poulet DG (Directeur Général)
ingredients: 3 ripe plantains, peeled and sliced diagonally
1/2 cup vegetable oil (for frying plantains and chicken)
Salt and black pepper to taste
instructions: Season the chicken pieces with garlic, ginger, one stock cube, salt, and pepper, then let marinate for at least 30 minutes.
Fry the plantain slices in hot oil until golden on both sides, then remove and drain on paper towels.
In the same or a separate pan, fry the marinated chicken pieces until golden brown and cooked through, then set aside.
In a large skillet, heat a little oil and sauté the onion, garlic, and ginger until fragrant, then add the chopped tomatoes and tomato paste and cook until reduced.
Add the sliced carrots and cook for 5 minutes until slightly softened, then add the bell peppers, remaining stock cube, and scotch bonnet, cooking briefly to keep the vegetables crisp.
Return the fried chicken to the skillet and toss to coat evenly in the sauce and vegetables.
Gently fold in the fried plantains, tossing carefully to combine without breaking them.
Serve hot as a festive main dish, garnished with the colorful peppers and carrots.

title: Eru
ingredients: 300g water leaves (or spinach as the closest common substitute), chopped
instructions: Boil the cow skin and stockfish together in water until tender, about 30 minutes, then set aside with a little of the cooking liquid.
In a large pot, combine the chopped water leaves with a small amount of water and cook over medium heat for about 10 minutes until wilted.
Add the shredded eru leaves to the pot along with the palm oil, stirring well to coat the leaves evenly.
Stir in the ground crayfish, smoked fish, cooked cow skin, stockfish, and stock cube.
Simmer over low heat for 20-25 minutes, stirring occasionally, adding reserved cooking liquid if the mixture becomes too dry.
Add scotch bonnet and adjust salt to taste, then simmer a final 5 minutes.
Serve hot with roasted or boiled plantains, or with garri (fufu corn).

title: Poulet à la Moambe (Chicken Moambe)
ingredients: 2 cups moambe (palm nut) cream/sauce, canned or extracted from fresh palm nuts
1 scotch bonnet or piri-piri pepper, chopped (optional)
2 tbsp palm oil (if needed to enrich sauce)
instructions: Season the chicken pieces with salt, garlic, and ginger, and let marinate briefly while preparing other ingredients.
In a large pot, brown the chicken pieces in a little palm oil over medium-high heat until lightly seared on all sides, then remove and set aside.
In the same pot, sauté the onion until soft and translucent, then add the chopped tomatoes, tomato paste, and bay leaf, cooking until the tomatoes break down.
Return the chicken to the pot and pour in the moambe (palm nut) cream, stirring to coat the chicken evenly.
Add the stock cubes and enough water to just cover the chicken, then bring to a simmer.
Cover and simmer gently over low heat for 35-45 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the chicken is tender and the sauce has thickened and turned a deep reddish-orange.
Add the scotch bonnet pepper in the last 10 minutes if using, and adjust salt to taste.
Serve hot over steamed rice or with fufu.

title: Fufu with Saka Saka (Cassava Leaves)
ingredients: 500g pounded/ground cassava leaves (saka saka, fresh or frozen)
instructions: To prepare the saka saka, boil the pounded cassava leaves in water for at least 45 minutes to 1 hour until tender, changing the water once if needed, then drain well.
In a pot, heat the palm oil and sauté the onion and garlic until fragrant.
Add the boiled cassava leaves, smoked fish, bouillon cube, and ground peanuts if using, stirring to combine.
Simmer over low heat for 15-20 minutes, adding a splash of water if the mixture is too dry, and season with salt and scotch bonnet to taste.
To prepare the fufu, bring the water to a boil, then gradually whisk in the cassava flour, stirring vigorously and continuously to avoid lumps.
Continue stirring and kneading the mixture with a wooden paddle over low heat until it forms a smooth, stretchy, thick dough, about 10 minutes.
Shape the fufu into smooth rounded balls using wet hands or a spoon.
Serve the fufu alongside the hot saka saka for scooping.

title: Liboke de Poisson (Fish Steamed in Leaves)
ingredients: 4 whole tilapia or mackerel, cleaned and scaled
Salt and black pepper to taste
Banana leaves, cleaned and softened over flame
Fresh herbs (such as bitter greens or parsley), chopped
instructions: Season the cleaned fish inside and out with salt, black pepper, crushed bouillon cube, garlic, and ginger, then let marinate for 15-20 minutes.
Lay out a large piece of softened banana leaf and place a fish in the center.
Top the fish with slices of onion, tomato, scotch bonnet, and a drizzle of palm oil, then sprinkle with chopped herbs.
Fold the banana leaf tightly around the fish to form a sealed parcel, securing with kitchen twine or a strip of the leaf itself; repeat for remaining fish.
Place the parcels in a steamer basket or on a rack over simmering water, or directly on a hot grill.
Steam or grill for 20-25 minutes, turning once, until the fish is cooked through and flakes easily.
Carefully unwrap the parcels at the table, being mindful of hot steam, and serve with the juices over rice or fufu.

title: Pondu (Cassava Leaf Stew)
ingredients: 500g pounded cassava leaves (pondu, fresh or frozen)
instructions: Place the pounded cassava leaves in a large pot with enough water to cover, and bring to a boil.
Reduce heat and simmer the leaves for 45 minutes to 1 hour until very tender, topping up water as needed.
Drain excess water, then stir in the palm oil, chopped onion, and garlic, cooking over medium heat for 10 minutes.
Add the ground peanuts, smoked fish, dried shrimp if using, and bouillon cube, stirring well to combine.
Simmer uncovered over low heat for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the stew thickens slightly.
Season with salt and scotch bonnet pepper to taste.
Serve hot with fufu, rice, or boiled plantains.

title: Jollof Rice (Cameroonian Style)
ingredients: 500g chicken pieces or beef, cut into chunks
1 scotch bonnet pepper, blended with tomatoes (optional)
Salt and curry powder to taste
instructions: Season the chicken or beef with garlic, ginger, one stock cube, and salt, then boil or fry until cooked through; reserve any broth.
In a large pot, heat the oil and sauté the chopped onion until translucent, then stir in the tomato paste and fry for 2-3 minutes.
Add the blended tomatoes, bell peppers, and scotch bonnet, and cook down over medium heat for 15-20 minutes until the sauce thickens and the raw tomato smell fades.
Add the cooked meat and its broth, bay leaves, remaining stock cube, curry powder, and salt, and simmer for 10 minutes.
Stir in the washed rice, ensuring it is well coated in the sauce, then add enough water or broth to just cover the rice.
Cover the pot tightly and cook over low heat for 25-30 minutes, stirring gently once or twice, until the rice is tender and has absorbed the sauce.
Let the rice rest off heat, covered, for 5 minutes before fluffing with a fork.
Serve hot, garnished with fried plantains or a side salad if desired.

title: Attiéké with Grilled Fish
ingredients: 4 whole tilapia or capitaine fillets, cleaned
instructions: Rub the fish with lemon juice, garlic, ginger, and salt, and let marinate for 30 minutes.
Heat a grill or grill pan and cook the fish over medium-high heat for 6-8 minutes per side until golden and cooked through.
While the fish grills, steam the attiéké by sprinkling it with a little water and warming it in a covered pot or steamer for about 10 minutes, fluffing with a fork.
In a separate pan, heat the oil and lightly sauté the onions, tomatoes, and bell pepper for 3-4 minutes until just softened, keeping them slightly crisp.
Season the vegetable mix with salt and add the scotch bonnet if using.
Mound the steamed attiéké on plates, place the grilled fish alongside, and top with the tomato-onion mixture.
Garnish with chopped parsley and serve with extra lemon wedges.

title: Kedjenou (Ivorian Chicken and Vegetable Stew)
ingredients: Salt and black pepper to taste
instructions: Place the chicken pieces in a canari (traditional clay pot) or a heavy-lidded pot along with the tomatoes, onion, bell pepper, and eggplant.
Add the garlic, ginger, whole scotch bonnet, bay leaves, palm oil, salt, and pepper without adding any water.
Cover the pot tightly with a lid to seal in the steam.
Cook over low heat, shaking the covered pot occasionally instead of stirring, so the ingredients release their own juices and simmer slowly.
Continue cooking for about 45-60 minutes, shaking every 10 minutes, until the chicken is tender and the vegetables have melted into a thick sauce.
Remove the whole scotch bonnet before serving.
Serve hot with attiéké, rice, or fufu.

title: Garba (Fried Tuna with Seasoned Attiéké)
instructions: Cut the tuna into large chunks and season with lime juice, curry powder, bouillon powder, and salt; let marinate for 20 minutes.
Heat the vegetable oil in a deep pan or pot until hot, then fry the tuna chunks in batches until deeply golden and crisp on the outside, about 4-5 minutes per batch.
Drain the fried tuna on paper towels.
Steam or moisten the attiéké with a bit of water and warm it through in a covered pot for 10 minutes.
Toss the diced tomatoes, chopped onion, and minced scotch bonnet together in a small bowl with a pinch of salt to make the fresh pepper relish.
Serve the fried tuna over the attiéké, topped generously with the tomato-onion-pepper relish.

title: Alloco (Fried Sweet Plantains)
ingredients: 4 ripe plantains, peeled and sliced diagonally
Skewers or toothpicks (optional, for street-style serving)
instructions: Peel the ripe plantains and slice them diagonally into pieces about 1/2 inch thick.
Heat the vegetable oil in a deep frying pan over medium-high heat.
Fry the plantain slices in batches, turning occasionally, until golden brown and caramelized on both sides, about 4-6 minutes.
Drain the fried plantains on paper towels and lightly salt them.
Mix the chopped onion, diced tomatoes, minced scotch bonnet, and grated ginger in a bowl to make the spicy onion sauce.
Serve the alloco hot, topped with the onion-tomato sauce, traditionally alongside grilled fish or hard-boiled eggs.

title: Sauce Graine (Palm Nut Sauce)
ingredients: 4 cups palm nut cream (extracted from fresh palm fruit or canned concentrate)
instructions: Season the beef chunks with salt, garlic, and ginger, then boil in water until tender, reserving the broth.
If using fresh palm fruit, boil and pound the fruit, then sieve it with water to extract the thick red palm nut cream; if using canned concentrate, dilute it with warm water.
In a large pot, combine the palm nut cream with the reserved beef broth, chopped onion, and tomatoes.
Bring to a simmer and cook uncovered, stirring occasionally, until the oil separates and rises to the top, about 40-50 minutes.
Add the cooked beef, smoked fish, and whole scotch bonnet pepper, and continue simmering for another 15-20 minutes.
Stir in fresh basil leaves if using, and adjust salt to taste.
Remove the whole pepper before serving and serve the sauce hot over boiled rice.

title: Foutou with Sauce Claire
ingredients: 1 lb fresh fish (such as tilapia), cleaned
instructions: Boil the chopped plantains and cassava together in water until very soft, about 25-30 minutes.
Drain the plantains and cassava, then pound them together in a large mortar with a pestle, adding a little of the cooking water as needed, until a smooth, stretchy dough (foutou) forms.
Shape the foutou into a smooth mound and set aside, keeping it covered and warm.
For the sauce claire, season and boil the beef in water until tender, then remove and reserve the broth.
In a pot, heat the oil and sauté the onion and garlic, then add the tomatoes and tomato paste, cooking until softened.
Pour in the reserved beef broth, add the beef and whole scotch bonnet, and simmer for 15 minutes.
Add the fish to the pot and simmer gently for another 10-12 minutes until the fish is cooked through, then season with salt.
Serve the foutou mound with the light tomato-based sauce ladled over or alongside.

title: Ivorian Braisé Fish (Poisson Braisé)
ingredients: 4 whole fish (such as sea bream or capitaine), cleaned and scored
instructions: Score the fish on both sides and rub with lime juice, garlic, ginger, bouillon powder, and salt; marinate for 30 minutes.
Heat the oil in a large skillet or grill pan and cook the fish over medium heat for 6-7 minutes per side until browned and cooked through.
Remove the fish and set aside, keeping warm.
In the same pan, sauté the onion, tomatoes, and bell pepper until softened, about 5 minutes.
Add the sliced scotch bonnet and season the vegetables with a little salt.
Return the fish to the pan, spoon the vegetables over the top, and simmer together for 3-4 minutes to combine flavors.
Serve hot with attiéké or rice.

title: Ivorian Riz Gras (Rice Cooked with Meat and Vegetables)
ingredients: 1/2 cup smoked fish, cleaned and flaked
Salt and bouillon powder to taste
instructions: Season the beef with garlic, salt, and bouillon powder, then boil in water until tender; reserve the broth.
Heat the oil in a large pot and sauté the onion until translucent.
Add the tomato paste and blended tomatoes, cooking down for 8-10 minutes to form a thick base.
Add the cooked beef, smoked fish, diced carrot, and whole scotch bonnet, stirring to combine.
Pour in the reserved beef broth plus enough water to cook the rice, and bring to a boil.
Stir in the rice, reduce heat to low, cover, and cook for 20-25 minutes until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed.
Fluff the rice gently and serve hot.

title: Tigadèguèna (Malian Peanut Stew)
ingredients: 2 cups sweet potatoes, peeled and cubed
instructions: Season the meat with salt and a little minced garlic, then brown it in the vegetable oil in a large pot over medium-high heat.
Add the chopped onion and cook until softened, about 5 minutes.
Stir in the tomato paste and chopped tomatoes, cooking for 8-10 minutes until the mixture darkens slightly.
Add enough water to cover the meat, bring to a simmer, and cook for 30 minutes until the meat begins to tenderize.
Dissolve the peanut butter in a cup of warm water, then stir it into the pot along with the whole scotch bonnet pepper.

Add the sweet potatoes and cabbage, and simmer uncovered for another 25-30 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent the peanut sauce from sticking, until the oil rises to the surface and the vegetables are tender.
Remove the whole pepper, adjust salt, and serve hot over rice.

title: Fonio with Vegetables (Malian Style)
instructions: Rinse the fonio briefly in cool water using a fine sieve, then drain well.
Bring the water to a boil in a pot, add a pinch of salt, then stir in the fonio.
Cover and cook over low heat for about 5 minutes, then remove from heat and let it steam, covered, for another 5 minutes; fluff with a fork.
In a separate pan, heat the oil and sauté the onion and garlic until fragrant.
Add the carrot, cabbage, and tomatoes, and cook for 8-10 minutes until the vegetables are tender.
Season the vegetables with salt, then fold them through the fluffed fonio.
Serve warm as a side dish or light main.

title: Capitaine Fish à la Malienne
ingredients: Salt and black pepper to taste
instructions: Rub the capitaine fillets with lime juice, garlic, ginger, salt, and black pepper, and let marinate for 20-30 minutes.
Heat the oil in a large skillet and sear the fish fillets for 3-4 minutes per side until golden; remove and set aside.
In the same skillet, sauté the onion until softened, then stir in the tomato paste and chopped tomatoes.
Cook the tomato mixture for 10 minutes until it thickens into a sauce, adding a splash of water if needed.
Add the chopped scotch bonnet and season the sauce with salt.
Return the fish to the skillet, spoon the sauce over it, cover, and simmer gently for 8-10 minutes until the fish is fully cooked.
Serve hot with rice or fonio.

title: Poulet Yassa (Malian Style)
ingredients: Salt and black pepper to taste
instructions: Marinate the chicken pieces in lime juice, mustard, minced garlic, salt, and pepper for at least 2 hours, or overnight in the refrigerator.
Remove the chicken from the marinade, reserving the liquid, and grill or pan-sear the chicken pieces until browned on all sides.
In a large pot, heat the oil and cook the sliced onions slowly over medium-low heat until deeply caramelized, about 25-30 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Add the reserved marinade, bay leaves, and whole scotch bonnet to the caramelized onions, and bring to a simmer.
Return the browned chicken to the pot, cover, and simmer for 25-30 minutes until the chicken is tender and infused with the tangy onion sauce.
Remove the whole pepper and bay leaves before serving.
Serve the chicken and onion sauce hot over rice.

title: Riz Gras Malien (Malian Rice with Meat)
ingredients: Salt and bouillon powder to taste
instructions: Season the meat with garlic, salt, and bouillon powder, then brown it in the oil in a large pot over medium-high heat.
Remove the meat and set aside, leaving the oil in the pot.
Sauté the onion in the same pot until softened, then add the tomato paste and blended tomatoes, cooking for 8-10 minutes.
Return the meat to the pot along with the carrot, cabbage, and whole scotch bonnet, and add enough water to cover.
Simmer for 30 minutes until the meat is tender, then remove the meat and vegetables, reserving the sauce and broth.
Stir the rice into the reserved broth, adding more water if needed to cook the rice, cover, and cook on low heat for 20-25 minutes.
Return the meat and vegetables to the pot, gently fold through the rice, and serve hot.

title: Maafe (Malian Peanut and Meat Stew)
ingredients: 2 cups butternut squash or pumpkin, cubed
instructions: Brown the beef in the vegetable oil in a large pot over medium-high heat, then remove and set aside.
Sauté the onion and garlic in the same pot until fragrant, then stir in the tomato paste and chopped tomatoes, cooking for 8 minutes.
Return the beef to the pot, add enough water to cover, and simmer for 30 minutes until the beef is tender.
Dissolve the peanut butter in a cup of warm water until smooth, then stir it into the stew along with the whole scotch bonnet.
Add the squash and simmer uncovered for 20 minutes, stirring occasionally so the peanut sauce doesn't stick to the bottom.
Add the okra and continue simmering for another 10 minutes until all the vegetables are tender and the sauce has thickened with the oil rising to the top.
Remove the whole pepper, season with salt, and serve hot over rice.

title: Fufu with Light Soup (Togolese Style)
ingredients: 1 lb goat meat or beef, cubed
instructions: Boil the cassava and yam together in water until very soft, about 30 minutes.
Drain, reserving a little cooking water, and pound the cassava and yam together in a mortar until a smooth, elastic dough forms; shape into a mound and set aside.
Season and boil the goat meat with garlic and salt until tender, reserving the broth.
In a pot, combine the broth with the chopped tomatoes, onion, and tomato paste, and simmer for 10 minutes.
Add the cooked meat, smoked fish, and whole scotch bonnet, and simmer for another 10 minutes.
Stir in the sliced okra and cook for 5 more minutes until the soup is lightly thickened but still light and broth-like.
Remove the whole pepper and serve the light soup alongside the fufu mound for pulling and dipping.

title: Akpan (Togolese Fermented Corn Pudding)
ingredients: 1 cup evaporated milk or fresh milk
instructions: Soak the corn in water for 2-3 days to ferment, then grind it into a smooth paste and sieve to remove the chaff, producing a fermented corn starch (this is traditionally prepared in advance).
Mix a portion of the sieved corn starch with cold water to form a smooth, lump-free slurry.
Bring the remaining water to a boil, then gradually pour in the slurry while stirring continuously.
Continue cooking and stirring over low heat until the mixture thickens into a smooth, semi-translucent pudding, about 8-10 minutes.
Pour the hot pudding into small bowls or cups and allow it to cool and set into a firm, jelly-like texture.
Chill the set akpan, then serve cold topped with milk and sugar to taste.

title: Ablo (Togolese Steamed Rice Cakes)
ingredients: 1 cup cooked mashed rice or leftover cooked rice
Banana leaves or corn husks, for steaming
instructions: Soak raw rice in water for 24 hours, then drain and grind it into a fine paste, allowing it to ferment for several hours to develop a mild tang (or use fermented rice flour as a shortcut).
Combine the rice flour or paste with the mashed cooked rice, sugar, yeast dissolved in warm water, and salt, mixing into a thick, smooth batter.
Cover the batter and let it rest in a warm place for 1-2 hours until slightly bubbly and risen.
Line small bowls, ramekins, or banana leaf cups with the batter, filling each about two-thirds full.
Arrange the filled molds in a steamer and steam over boiling water for 20-25 minutes until the cakes are set and a skewer comes out clean.
Allow to cool slightly before unmolding.
Serve the soft, tangy rice cakes warm alongside a spicy pepper sauce or bean stew.

title: Pâte with Sauce Tomate (Togolese Corn Pâte)
ingredients: 1 lb beef or chicken, cut into pieces
Salt and bouillon powder to taste
instructions: Season the meat with garlic, salt, and bouillon powder, then boil in water until tender; reserve the broth.
To make the pâte, mix a portion of the corn flour with cold water to form a smooth paste.
Bring the remaining water to a boil, then stir in the corn paste, whisking continuously to avoid lumps.
Reduce heat to low and continue stirring vigorously with a wooden spoon for 8-10 minutes until the mixture becomes thick, smooth, and stretchy; shape into a mound and set aside.
For the sauce, heat the oil in a pot and sauté the onion until soft, then add the tomato paste and blended tomatoes, cooking for 10 minutes.
Add the cooked meat, reserved broth, and whole scotch bonnet, and simmer for 15-20 minutes until the sauce thickens.
Remove the whole pepper, season with salt, and serve the tomato sauce alongside the pâte.

title: Togolese Riz au Gras
ingredients: Salt and bouillon powder to taste
instructions: Season the beef with garlic, salt, and bouillon powder, then brown it in the oil in a large pot.
Remove the beef and set aside, then sauté the onion in the same pot until translucent.
Add the tomato paste and blended tomatoes, cooking down for 8-10 minutes into a thick base.
Return the beef to the pot with the carrot, cabbage, and whole scotch bonnet, and add enough water to cover everything.
Simmer for 30 minutes until the beef is tender, then remove the solids, reserving the flavored broth.
Stir the rice into the broth, adding water as needed, cover, and cook on low heat for 20-25 minutes until tender.
Fold the beef and vegetables back through the rice and serve hot.

title: Amiwo (Beninese Corn Pâte with Tomato Sauce)
ingredients: 1 lb fish or chicken, cut into pieces
Salt and bouillon powder to taste
instructions: Season and cook the fish or chicken with garlic, salt, and bouillon powder until tender; reserve the cooking liquid.
Mix a portion of the corn flour with cold water to make a smooth paste.
Bring the remaining water to a boil, whisk in the corn paste, then reduce heat and stir vigorously for 8-10 minutes until thick, smooth, and stretchy to form the amiwo pâte.
Stir the palm oil directly into the hot pâte until it takes on a rich reddish-orange color, then shape into a mound.
In a separate pot, sauté the onion, then add the tomato paste and blended tomatoes, cooking for 10 minutes.
Add the cooked fish or chicken, reserved broth, and whole scotch bonnet, and simmer for 15 minutes until thickened.
Remove the whole pepper, season with salt, and serve the tomato sauce alongside the amiwo.

title: Akassa (Beninese Fermented Corn Dumplings)
ingredients: 3 cups white corn, soaked and fermented
Kitchen twine or raffia, for tying parcels
instructions: Soak the corn in water for 2-3 days until fermented, then drain and grind into a smooth paste.
Sieve the ground corn with water to remove the bran, collecting the smooth fermented corn starch liquid.
Let the starch settle, then pour off the excess water, keeping the thick sediment.
Cook a portion of the starch with a little water over low heat, stirring to form a thick base paste.
Mix this cooked base back into the remaining raw starch, stirring vigorously until fully combined and smooth.
Wrap portions of the mixture in banana leaves or corn husks, tying them securely.
Steam or boil the wrapped akassa for 30-40 minutes until firm and set, then let cool slightly before unwrapping and serving.

title: Wagasi Fried with Tomato Sauce
ingredients: 1 lb wagasi cheese (Beninese Fulani cheese), sliced
instructions: Heat the vegetable oil in a skillet over medium heat.
Fry the sliced wagasi cheese for 2-3 minutes per side until golden brown and slightly crisp on the outside; remove and set aside.
In the same skillet, sauté the onion and garlic until fragrant.
Add the ginger, tomato paste, and chopped tomatoes, and cook for 10 minutes until the sauce thickens.
Stir in the chopped scotch bonnet and season with salt.
Return the fried wagasi to the skillet, gently folding it into the sauce, and simmer together for 3-4 minutes.
Serve hot with rice or as a side dish.

title: Sauce d'Arachide (Beninese Peanut Sauce)
ingredients: 2 cups spinach or bitter leaf, chopped
Cooked rice or pâte, for serving
instructions: Season the meat with garlic and salt, then boil in water until tender, reserving the broth.
Heat the palm oil in a pot and sauté the onion until softened.
Add the tomato paste and chopped tomatoes, cooking for 8-10 minutes until thickened.
Dissolve the peanut butter in a cup of the reserved broth until smooth, then stir it into the pot along with the remaining broth and whole scotch bonnet.
Add the cooked meat and simmer uncovered for 20-25 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking, until the oil rises to the surface.
Stir in the chopped spinach or bitter leaf and cook for another 5 minutes.
Remove the whole pepper, season with salt, and serve hot with rice or pâte.

title: Moyo (Beninese Tomato and Pepper Relish)
ingredients: 2 tbsp vegetable oil or palm oil
1 tbsp fresh chopped parsley or basil (optional)
instructions: Finely chop the tomatoes and onion and place them together in a mixing bowl.
Add the minced scotch bonnet pepper to the bowl, adjusting quantity to the desired heat level.
Drizzle in the oil and lime juice, then season with salt.
Mix everything thoroughly, mashing the tomatoes slightly with the back of a spoon to release their juices and create a chunky relish.
Let the mixture sit for 10-15 minutes to allow the flavors to meld.
Stir in fresh parsley or basil if using.
Serve moyo as a fresh condiment alongside grilled fish, meat, or fried plantains.

title: Injera
ingredients: 5 cups water, plus more for thinning
1/4 cup active injera starter (ersho) or plain water with a pinch of active yeast
1 tbsp all-purpose flour (optional, to aid fermentation)
instructions: Whisk teff flour and water together in a large non-metallic bowl until a smooth, thin batter forms.
Stir in the ersho starter if using, cover loosely, and leave at room temperature for 2 to 3 days to ferment until bubbly and slightly sour-smelling.
After fermentation, pour off the clear liquid that rises to the top and stir the remaining thick batter, adding water to reach a thin, pourable consistency, then add salt.
Heat a large flat clay mitad or nonstick skillet over medium heat without oil.
Pour a thin layer of batter in a spiral motion starting from the outer edge and working inward to cover the surface completely.
Cover with a lid and cook for 1 to 2 minutes until the surface is covered with small holes (eyes) and the edges lift; injera is cooked only on one side and should not be flipped.
Slide the injera onto a clean cloth or tray to cool, then stack with cloth or plastic between layers to prevent sticking.
Repeat with remaining batter and serve as the base and accompaniment for wats and other stews.

title: Doro Wat
ingredients: 1 whole chicken (about 1.5 kg), cut into pieces
instructions: Rub chicken pieces with lemon juice and salt, then rinse and set aside.
In a large heavy pot, cook the minced onions over medium-low heat with no oil, stirring frequently, until they soften and reduce down, about 20 minutes.
Add the niter kibbeh and continue cooking the onions until deeply golden.
Stir in berbere, garlic, and ginger, and cook for several minutes until fragrant and the oil separates slightly.
Add water or stock to form a thick sauce and simmer for 10 minutes.
Add the chicken pieces, turning to coat in the sauce, cover, and simmer for 35 to 40 minutes until the chicken is tender, stirring occasionally.
Pierce the hard-boiled eggs a few times with a knife and add them to the pot for the last 10 minutes so they absorb the sauce.
Adjust salt and serve hot with injera.

title: Kitfo
ingredients: 500 g very fresh, high-quality lean beef tenderloin, finely minced
3 tbsp niter kibbeh, warmed until liquid
1 tsp koseret (dried herb) or substitute dried basil
Ayib (fresh Ethiopian cottage cheese), for serving
instructions: Trim the beef of any sinew and mince it very finely by hand with a sharp knife until almost paste-like.
Warm the niter kibbeh gently until fully melted and fragrant.
In a bowl, combine the minced beef with mitmita, koseret, and salt.
Pour the warm niter kibbeh over the meat and mix thoroughly until evenly coated.

Traditionally kitfo is served raw (leb leb, lightly warmed) at this point; for a cooked version, quickly warm the mixture in a pan over low heat just until barely warmed through, stirring constantly, without fully cooking.
Serve mounded on a plate alongside a scoop of ayib and cooked gomen.
Accompany with fresh injera for scooping.

title: Shiro Wat
ingredients: 3 tbsp niter kibbeh or vegetable oil
1 tbsp berbere spice blend (optional, for extra heat)
instructions: Heat niter kibbeh or oil in a pot over medium heat and saute the onion until soft and translucent.
Add garlic and ginger and cook for another minute until fragrant.
Stir in the chopped tomato and cook until it breaks down slightly.
Add berbere if using and stir to combine with the onion mixture.
Pour in water and bring to a gentle boil.
Reduce heat to low and slowly whisk in the shiro powder to avoid lumps, stirring continuously.
Simmer for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring often, until the sauce thickens to a smooth, pourable consistency, adding more water if needed.
Season with salt and serve hot with injera.

title: Misir Wot
ingredients: 3 tbsp niter kibbeh or vegetable oil
instructions: Heat the niter kibbeh or oil in a large pot and cook the minced onion over medium heat until soft and golden, about 10 minutes.
Add garlic and ginger and cook for another minute.
Stir in the berbere and tomato paste and cook for 2 to 3 minutes until fragrant and the oil separates.
Add the rinsed lentils and stir to coat evenly in the spiced onion mixture.
Pour in water, bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer uncovered, stirring occasionally.
Cook for 20 to 25 minutes, adding more water as needed, until the lentils are soft and the stew has thickened.
Season with salt to taste and serve hot with injera.

title: Tibs
ingredients: 600 g beef sirloin or lamb, cut into small cubes
1 to 2 green chilies (jalapeno or serrano), sliced
instructions: Heat niter kibbeh in a heavy skillet or pan over high heat until hot.
Add the meat cubes and sear quickly, stirring frequently, until browned on the outside, 5 to 7 minutes.
Add the sliced onion and cook for a few minutes until it begins to soften.
Stir in garlic, ginger, and green chilies and cook for another 2 minutes.
Add the chopped tomato and berbere if using, and cook until the tomato softens and the flavors meld, about 5 minutes.
Continue cooking over high heat, stirring frequently, until the meat is cooked through but still tender, and most liquid has evaporated.
Season with salt, garnish with dried rosemary if using, and serve hot with injera.

title: Gomen
ingredients: 1 large bunch collard greens, stems removed and leaves chopped
3 tbsp niter kibbeh or vegetable oil
instructions: Wash the collard greens thoroughly and blanch briefly in boiling water, then drain and chop finely.
Heat niter kibbeh or oil in a large pot over medium heat and saute the onion until soft and translucent.
Add garlic, ginger, and green chilies if using, and cook for another minute until fragrant.
Add the chopped collard greens to the pot and stir well to coat with the onion mixture.
Cover and cook over low to medium heat for 20 to 30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the greens are very tender.
Season with salt to taste and serve warm as a side with injera and other wats.

title: Ugali with Sukuma Wiki
ingredients: 1 bunch sukuma wiki (collard greens or kale), finely shredded
instructions: Bring 3 cups of the water to a boil in a heavy-bottomed pot.
Mix the remaining 1 cup of water with the maize flour to form a smooth paste, then stir it into the boiling water.
Cook, stirring constantly with a wooden spoon, until it begins to thicken.
Reduce heat to low and gradually add more maize flour, stirring vigorously and pressing out lumps, until the ugali becomes very stiff and pulls away from the sides of the pot.
Cover and cook on low heat for a few more minutes, then turn out onto a plate and shape into a smooth mound.
For the sukuma wiki, heat oil in a separate pan and saute the onion until soft, then add the tomato and cook until it breaks down.
Add the shredded greens, season with salt, and cook for 5 to 8 minutes, stirring occasionally, until tender but still bright green.
Serve the ugali alongside the sukuma wiki.

title: Nyama Choma
ingredients: 1.5 kg goat meat or beef, cut into large bone-in pieces
Kachumbari (tomato and onion salad), for serving
instructions: Rub the meat pieces with salt, pepper, oil, and garlic if using, and let marinate for at least 30 minutes.
Prepare a charcoal grill or open fire and let it burn down to hot embers.
Place the meat on the grill over the hot coals, positioning bone-in pieces where they will cook evenly.
Grill slowly, turning frequently, for 45 minutes to over an hour depending on the cut, until the outside is well charred and the meat is cooked through and tender.
Baste occasionally with a little oil to prevent drying out.
Once cooked, remove from the grill and chop into smaller pieces on a wooden board.
Serve hot with kachumbari and lemon wedges on the side.

title: Githeri
ingredients: 2 cups dried maize (corn) kernels, soaked overnight
1 cup dried beans (such as kidney or pinto), soaked overnight
instructions: Drain the soaked maize and beans and place them together in a large pot with fresh water to cover generously.
Bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer for 1.5 to 2 hours, topping up water as needed, until both the maize and beans are tender.
In a separate pan, heat the oil and saute the onion until golden.
Add the tomato and carrots if using, and cook until softened.
Stir in curry powder if using, then add this mixture to the cooked maize and beans.
Simmer everything together for another 10 to 15 minutes so the flavors combine, mashing some of the mixture lightly if a thicker consistency is desired.
Season with salt to taste and serve hot.

title: Pilau
ingredients: 500 g beef or goat meat, cut into chunks
1 tbsp pilau masala (whole spice blend of cumin, cloves, cardamom, cinnamon, black pepper)
instructions: Heat oil or ghee in a large heavy pot and fry the sliced onions over medium heat until deep golden brown.
Add the meat and brown it well on all sides.
Stir in the pilau masala, garlic, and ginger, and cook for a few minutes until fragrant.
Add the chopped tomatoes and cook until they soften into the mixture.
Pour in the stock, season with salt, cover, and simmer until the meat is tender, about 45 minutes to 1 hour.
Add the rinsed rice to the pot, stirring gently to combine with the meat and liquid, adding more stock or water so the liquid sits just above the rice.
Bring to a boil, then cover tightly and reduce heat to low, cooking for 20 minutes until the rice is tender and liquid is absorbed.
Let rest off the heat for 5 minutes, then fluff gently with a fork before serving.

title: Mukimo
ingredients: 1 cup pumpkin leaves or spinach, chopped
instructions: Place the potatoes, maize, and peas or beans in a large pot with enough water to cover, and bring to a boil.
Simmer until the potatoes and maize are tender, about 20 to 25 minutes.
Add the chopped pumpkin leaves or spinach during the last 5 minutes of cooking to wilt them.
Drain most of the water, reserving a little, and mash everything together in the pot using a wooden masher or spoon until well combined and relatively smooth.
In a small pan, saute the onion in butter or oil until golden, then fold it into the mashed mixture.
Season with salt to taste, mixing thoroughly.
Serve warm, traditionally alongside stewed meat or vegetables.

title: Mandazi
instructions: In a large bowl, whisk together flour, sugar, cardamom, baking powder, and salt.
Add the coconut milk and melted butter, mixing until a soft, slightly sticky dough forms.
Knead the dough gently on a floured surface for a few minutes until smooth, then cover and let rest for 30 minutes.
Roll the dough out to about 1 cm thickness and cut into triangles or diamond shapes.
Heat oil in a deep pot to medium heat (not too hot, so the mandazi cook through).
Fry the pieces in batches, turning occasionally, until golden brown and puffed, about 3 to 5 minutes per batch.
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels.
Serve warm on their own or with tea.

title: Wali wa Nazi (Coconut Rice)
ingredients: 3 cups basmati or long-grain rice, rinsed
1 tbsp cooking oil or coconut oil
instructions: Rinse the rice thoroughly until the water runs clear, then drain well.
In a heavy-bottomed pot, combine the coconut milk, water, salt, and sugar if using, and bring to a gentle simmer.
Add the rinsed rice and oil, stirring once to combine.
Bring to a boil, then reduce the heat to low and cover tightly.
Cook undisturbed for 18 to 20 minutes, or until the rice is tender and the liquid has been fully absorbed.
Remove from heat and let stand covered for 5 minutes.
Fluff gently with a fork before serving, traditionally alongside fish, meat stew, or beans.

title: Chapati
ingredients: 1/4 cup vegetable oil, plus more for cooking and layering
instructions: In a large bowl, mix flour, salt, and sugar together.
Gradually add warm water and knead into a soft, pliable dough, then knead in a little oil until smooth.
Cover the dough and let it rest for 20 to 30 minutes.
Divide the dough into equal balls, roll each one out thinly, brush lightly with oil, and roll or fold it up into a coil to create layers, then let rest briefly.
Roll each coiled ball out again into a thin, flat round.
Heat a dry skillet or griddle over medium heat and cook each chapati for 1 to 2 minutes per side, brushing with a little oil, until golden brown spots appear and it is cooked through and flaky.
Stack cooked chapatis under a cloth to keep warm and soft.
Serve warm alongside stews, beans, or tea.

title: Mchicha
ingredients: 1 large bunch mchicha (amaranth greens) or spinach, washed and chopped
instructions: Heat oil in a pan over medium heat and saute the onion until soft and translucent.
Add garlic if using and cook briefly until fragrant.
Add the chopped tomatoes and cook until they soften and release their juices.
Add the chopped greens and stir well to combine with the tomato mixture, cooking until they begin to wilt.
Pour in the coconut milk, reduce heat to low, and simmer for 10 to 15 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the greens are tender and the sauce has slightly thickened.
Season with salt to taste and serve warm as a side dish with ugali or rice.

title: Ndizi na Nyama
ingredients: 6 green (unripe) bananas or plantains, peeled and cut into chunks
instructions: Heat oil in a large pot and brown the beef pieces on all sides over medium-high heat.
Add the chopped onion and garlic and cook until softened.
Stir in the tomatoes and curry powder, cooking until the tomatoes break down into a thick base.
Add enough water to cover the meat, bring to a boil, then reduce heat and simmer covered until the beef is tender, about 45 minutes.
Add the green banana or plantain chunks to the pot and continue simmering for 15 to 20 minutes until they are tender.
Pour in the coconut milk and simmer gently for another 10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the sauce thickens slightly.
Season with salt to taste and serve hot.

title: Matoke
instructions: Peel the green bananas carefully and place them whole or halved in a pot, traditionally lined with banana leaves.
Add just enough water or stock to come partway up the bananas without fully submerging them.
Cover tightly and steam over medium-low heat for 45 minutes to 1 hour, checking occasionally, until the bananas are very soft.
In a separate pan, heat oil and saute the onion until soft, then add the tomatoes and cook until they break down into a sauce, seasoning with salt.
Mash the steamed bananas roughly in the pot using a wooden spoon until they form a coarse, thick mash.
Fold the tomato and onion sauce into the mashed matoke, or serve it spooned over the top.
Serve warm as a staple alongside meat, groundnut sauce, or beans.

title: Luwombo
ingredients: 1 kg chicken or beef, cut into pieces
1 cup groundnut (peanut) paste or smoked dried fish as alternative filling
Banana leaves, cleaned and softened over flame
instructions: Heat oil in a pot and saute the onions until soft, then add the tomatoes and curry powder, cooking until a thick sauce forms.
Add the meat to the sauce along with a little water, season with salt, and partially cook for about 15 minutes, then stir in the groundnut paste.
Soften the banana leaves by passing them briefly over an open flame or dipping in hot water so they become pliable without tearing.
Spoon the meat and sauce mixture into the center of the banana leaves and fold tightly into a secure parcel, tying with banana fiber or string.
Place the wrapped parcel into a large pot, add water around (not into) the parcel, cover, and steam over low heat for 1.5 to 2 hours.
Check occasionally to ensure water does not run dry, topping up as needed.
Carefully unwrap the parcel and serve the stew hot, traditionally with matoke or rice.

title: Rolex
instructions: Beat the eggs in a bowl and mix in the chopped tomato, onion, and green pepper, seasoning with salt and pepper.
Heat a little oil in a flat pan or griddle over medium heat.
Pour the egg mixture into the pan, spreading it into a thin, even omelet, and cook until just set on the bottom.
Place a chapati directly on top of the cooking omelet in the pan, pressing gently so it sticks to the egg.
Flip the combined chapati and omelet together and cook briefly on the other side.
Add shredded cabbage on top if using, then roll the chapati and omelet up tightly into a log.
Slice in half and serve warm, typically wrapped in paper as a portable snack.

title: Waakye
ingredients: 1 handful dried waakye leaves (sorghum leaves) or 1/2 tsp baking soda
1 onion, sliced (for accompanying shito or stew)
instructions: Soak the black-eyed peas in water for a few hours, then rinse and place in a large pot with 4 cups of water.
Add the dried waakye leaves (or baking soda as a substitute) to the pot; this is what gives waakye its characteristic reddish-brown color.
Bring to a boil and cook the beans for about 30-40 minutes until they are tender but not mushy.
Remove the leaves once the water has turned a deep red-brown color, then rinse the rice and add it to the same pot along with the salt.
Add the additional 3 cups of water as needed, cover, and cook on medium-low heat until the rice and beans are fully cooked and the water is absorbed, about 25-30 minutes.
Fluff with a fork and serve hot, traditionally with shito, gari, spaghetti, boiled egg, avocado, and stewed meat or fish.

title: Banku and Tilapia
ingredients: 2 tbsp vegetable oil for frying fish
2 fresh chili peppers, for pepper sauce
instructions: Season the cleaned tilapia with salt and let it sit for 10 minutes, then either grill over charcoal or shallow-fry in oil until golden and cooked through on both sides.
In a heavy pot, combine the fermented corn dough and cassava dough with water, whisking to remove lumps.
Place the pot over medium heat and stir constantly with a wooden turning stick (banku stick) as the mixture thickens.
Continue stirring and folding the mixture vigorously for 15-20 minutes until it becomes smooth, stretchy, and fully cooked through with no raw starch taste.
Using a wet spoon or hand, mold the banku into smooth round balls and set aside.
Blend the tomato and chili peppers with a pinch of salt and onion to make a fresh pepper sauce (or use ground pepper mixed with sliced onion and a splash of oil).
Serve the banku alongside the fried or grilled tilapia and pepper sauce.

title: Kelewele
ingredients: 1 tsp cayenne pepper or ground pepper
instructions: Peel the ripe plantains and cut them into bite-sized diagonal cubes.
In a bowl, mix the grated ginger, minced garlic, cayenne pepper, ground cloves, salt, and anise seeds with a splash of water to form a seasoning paste.
Toss the plantain cubes thoroughly in the spice paste, making sure every piece is coated, and let marinate for 10-15 minutes.
Heat the vegetable oil in a deep pan or pot until hot but not smoking.
Carefully fry the plantain pieces in batches until deep golden brown and caramelized on the edges, about 4-5 minutes per batch.
Remove with a slotted spoon and drain on paper towels.
Serve hot, traditionally with roasted peanuts.

title: Red Red
ingredients: 1 ripe plantain, sliced and fried, for serving
instructions: Soak the black-eyed peas briefly, then rinse and boil in water until tender, about 30-40 minutes, then drain and reserve some cooking liquid.
Heat the palm oil in a separate pot until it becomes fragrant and slightly red in color.
Add the chopped onion and sauté until softened, then stir in the ginger and garlic if using.
Add the chopped tomatoes, tomato paste, and scotch bonnet pepper, cooking down until the mixture thickens into a rich sauce.
Stir in the ground crayfish and salt, then fold in the cooked black-eyed peas along with a little reserved cooking liquid to reach a stew-like consistency.
Simmer for 10-15 minutes to let the flavors meld.
Serve hot with slices of fried ripe plantain.

title: Fufu and Light Soup
ingredients: 500g goat meat or beef, cut into chunks
1 handful of garden eggs (African eggplant), optional
instructions: Boil the cassava and plantain together in water until very soft, about 25-30 minutes.
Drain the cassava and plantain, then pound together in a mortar with a pestle, folding and pounding until smooth, stretchy, and lump-free; shape into smooth balls (fufu).
Meanwhile, season the meat with salt, ginger, and garlic, then boil in a separate pot until tender, reserving the meat stock.
In the meat stock, add the blended tomatoes, chopped onion, tomato paste, and ground pepper, and simmer to make a light, thin, tomato-based broth (light soup).
Add the garden eggs and cook until soft, then stir in the kontomire or spinach if using and simmer a few more minutes.
Return the cooked meat to the soup and simmer until everything is well combined.
Serve the hot fufu balls in a bowl with the light soup ladled over or alongside.

title: Kenkey
ingredients: 1 cup raw uncooked corn dough (for the outer covering)
Dried corn husks or plantain leaves, for wrapping
instructions: Allow the corn dough to ferment for 2-3 days until it develops a slightly sour aroma.
Divide the fermented dough into two portions; cook one portion in a pot with water over medium heat, stirring continuously until it thickens into a stiff, partially cooked paste (aflata).
Mix the cooked aflata back into the remaining raw fermented dough along with salt, kneading until smooth and well combined.
Wrap portions of the mixture tightly in corn husks or plantain leaves, folding and tying securely into individual parcels.
Arrange the wrapped parcels in a large pot, add water to about halfway up the parcels, and steam-boil for 1.5 to 2 hours, topping up water as needed.
Remove the kenkey balls and let cool slightly before unwrapping.
Serve with pepper sauce, shito, or fried fish.

title: Jollof Rice (Ghanaian style)
instructions: Heat the vegetable oil in a large heavy-bottomed pot and sauté the chopped onion until translucent.

Add the blended tomatoes, tomato paste, blended red bell pepper, and scotch bonnet pepper, and fry the mixture on medium heat, stirring frequently, until the oil separates and rises to the top and the raw tomato smell is gone, about 15-20 minutes.
Stir in the curry powder, thyme, bay leaves, and salt, then add the stock and bring to a boil.
Wash the rice well and add it to the pot, stirring to combine with the sauce.
Reduce the heat to low, cover the pot tightly (traditionally with foil under the lid to trap steam), and allow the rice to cook slowly, stirring occasionally from the bottom to prevent sticking.
Cook until the rice is tender and has absorbed the sauce, developing a slightly smoky bottom layer (the prized 'bottom pot' flavor), about 30-40 minutes.
Fluff gently and serve hot with fried chicken, beef, or salad.

title: Groundnut Soup
ingredients: 500g chicken or goat meat, cut into pieces
instructions: Season the meat with salt and ginger, then boil in a pot with enough water until tender, reserving the stock.
In a separate bowl, dilute the groundnut paste with some warm water or stock to form a smooth, pourable liquid.
In the pot with the meat and stock, add the chopped onion, blended tomatoes, tomato paste, and scotch bonnet pepper, and bring to a simmer.
Stir in the diluted groundnut paste gradually, stirring constantly to prevent lumps or curdling.
Add the garden eggs if using, and simmer the soup on low-medium heat for 20-25 minutes, stirring occasionally, until it thickens and the oil from the peanuts rises to the surface.
Adjust seasoning with salt as needed.
Serve hot with rice balls, fufu, or banku.

title: Palava Sauce
ingredients: 1 large bunch kontomire (cocoyam leaves) or spinach, chopped
200g beef or goat meat, cooked and cubed
instructions: Wash and finely chop the kontomire leaves (or spinach), then set aside.
Heat the palm oil in a pot and sauté the chopped onion until soft.
Add the ground egusi seeds to the oil, stirring continuously to toast slightly and form small clumps.
Add the cooked meat, smoked fish, chopped scotch bonnet pepper, and ground crayfish, stirring to combine.
Pour in a little water or stock and simmer for 10 minutes to let the egusi cook through.
Add the chopped kontomire leaves, cover, and cook for another 10-15 minutes until the leaves are tender and the sauce has thickened.
Season with salt and serve hot with boiled yam, plantain, or rice.

title: Tuo Zaafi
ingredients: 2 cups rice flour or millet flour
1 tbsp cassava starch (optional, for extra smoothness)
1 bunch ayoyo leaves or kontomire, for soup
instructions: Bring the water to a boil in a heavy pot, then gradually whisk in the rice or millet flour to avoid lumps.
Stir continuously with a wooden spoon over medium heat as the mixture thickens into a smooth, stretchy paste.
Continue cooking and stirring, adding more flour or water to adjust consistency, until the tuo zaafi is smooth and elastic, about 15-20 minutes.
Shape into a mound and set aside, keeping it warm.
For the accompanying soup, cook the ayoyo leaves or kontomire in water with the dawadawa seasoning until soft and slightly slimy.
Stir in the ground egusi seeds, cooked smoked fish or beef, and salt, and simmer for 10 minutes until the soup thickens.
Serve the tuo zaafi with the soup ladled over or in a separate bowl for dipping.

title: Shito
ingredients: 1/2 cup dried fish (herring or mackerel), ground
3 dried bay leaves or 1 tsp ground cloves
instructions: Heat the vegetable oil in a heavy pot over medium heat.
Add the chopped onions and fry gently until deeply softened and starting to caramelize, about 10 minutes.
Stir in the minced garlic and ginger, cooking until fragrant and slightly golden.
Add the ground dried shrimp and ground dried fish, stirring well and frying for several minutes to release their aroma.
Mix in the ground chili pepper, tomato paste, and bay leaves or cloves, and reduce the heat to low.
Simmer slowly, stirring frequently to prevent burning, for 30-45 minutes until the mixture turns a deep black-brown color and the oil separates.
Season with salt, let cool, then transfer to a clean jar; shito keeps well refrigerated and is served as a condiment with waakye, kenkey, or rice.

title: Kontomire Stew
ingredients: 1/2 cup cooked cubed beef or goat meat (optional)
instructions: Wash the kontomire leaves thoroughly and chop finely; set aside.
Heat the palm oil in a pot and sauté the chopped onion until softened and translucent.
Add the chopped tomatoes and scotch bonnet pepper, cooking down until they soften into a light sauce.
Stir in the smoked fish, ground crayfish, and cooked meat if using, combining well.
Add the chopped kontomire leaves along with a small amount of water, cover, and simmer on medium-low heat for 20-25 minutes until the leaves are tender.
Stir occasionally, seasoning with salt to taste.
Serve hot with boiled yam, plantain, rice, or fufu.

title: Ampesi with Garden Egg Stew
ingredients: 2 medium yams, peeled and cut into chunks
2 ripe plantains, peeled and cut into chunks
200g smoked fish or salted fish, deboned
instructions: Place the yam and plantain chunks in a pot of salted water and boil until fork-tender, about 20-25 minutes.
Meanwhile, boil the chopped garden eggs in a separate small pot until soft, then drain and mash roughly with a wooden spoon.
Heat the palm oil in a pan and sauté the chopped onion until soft.
Add the scotch bonnet pepper, ground crayfish, and smoked fish, stirring to combine and frying for a few minutes.
Fold in the mashed garden eggs and simmer for 10 minutes, adding a splash of water if the stew is too thick.
Drain the boiled yam and plantain (ampesi) and serve hot alongside the garden egg stew.

title: Ga Kenkey with Fried Fish and Pepper Sauce
ingredients: 4 balls Ga kenkey (fermented corn dough dumplings)
4 small whole fish (tilapia or herring), cleaned
instructions: Season the cleaned fish with salt and let rest for 10 minutes.
Heat the vegetable oil in a deep frying pan and fry the fish until crisp and golden on both sides, then drain on paper towels.
Roast or boil the tomatoes, one onion, and chili peppers until softened.
Blend or pound the roasted tomatoes, onion, and peppers together with the ground crayfish and a pinch of salt to form a chunky fresh pepper sauce.
Slice the remaining raw onion thinly and stir into the pepper sauce for extra bite.
Unwrap the Ga kenkey balls from their corn husk wrapping.
Serve the kenkey with the fried fish and fresh pepper sauce on the side.

title: Aboboi (Ghanaian Rice Balls with Peanut Soup)
instructions: Cook the rice with extra water until very soft and slightly overcooked, then mash and mold into smooth round rice balls while still warm.
Season the chicken with salt and ginger, then boil in a pot until tender, reserving the stock.
In the same pot, add the chopped onion, blended tomatoes, tomato paste, and scotch bonnet pepper, and simmer for 10 minutes.
Dilute the peanut paste with warm stock until smooth, then stir it gradually into the simmering pot.
Cook on low-medium heat, stirring frequently, for 20-25 minutes until the soup thickens and the oil rises to the top.
Return the chicken pieces to the soup and simmer a few more minutes to combine flavors.
Serve the peanut soup hot with the rice balls.

title: Thieboudienne
ingredients: 3 cups broken rice or long-grain rice
1 kg firm white fish (grouper or sea bass), cut into steaks
1 small cassava, peeled and cut into chunks
2 cloves garlic and parsley, blended (for stuffing)
instructions: Make small pockets in the fish steaks and stuff them with a blended mixture of garlic, parsley, and a little chili (this stuffing is called rof).
Heat the oil in a large pot and briefly sear the stuffed fish pieces on both sides, then remove and set aside.
In the same pot, sauté the chopped onions until soft, then add the chopped tomatoes and tomato paste, cooking until it forms a thick red sauce.
Add water to the pot to create a broth, then add the cabbage, carrots, cassava, and whole scotch bonnet pepper, and simmer until the vegetables are tender.
Return the fish to the pot and simmer gently until cooked through, then carefully remove the fish and vegetables, reserving the flavorful broth.
Wash the rice and cook it in the reserved broth, adding broth gradually and stirring occasionally, until the rice is tender and has absorbed the deep red-orange color and flavor of the broth.
Serve the rice on a large platter topped with the fish and vegetables.

title: Yassa Poulet
ingredients: 1/2 cup fresh lemon or lime juice
3 cups cooked white rice, for serving
instructions: In a large bowl, combine the chicken pieces with the sliced onions, lemon juice, mustard, minced garlic, salt, and black pepper, and marinate for at least 2 hours or overnight in the refrigerator.
Remove the chicken from the marinade, reserving the onions and liquid, and grill or pan-sear the chicken pieces until browned on all sides.
In a large pot, heat the vegetable oil and sauté the reserved marinated onions until deeply caramelized and golden, about 15-20 minutes.
Add the reserved marinade liquid, bay leaves, and whole scotch bonnet pepper to the pot, and bring to a simmer.
Return the browned chicken to the pot and simmer gently for 25-30 minutes until the chicken is fully cooked and tender, with the onions forming a rich, tangy sauce.
Adjust seasoning with salt and pepper as needed.
Serve hot over steamed white rice.

title: Mafe (Maafe)
ingredients: 1 kg beef or lamb, cut into chunks
instructions: Heat the oil in a large heavy pot and brown the meat chunks on all sides.
Add the chopped onion and sauté until softened, then stir in the chopped tomatoes and tomato paste, cooking until thickened.
Pour in the water or stock, add the whole scotch bonnet pepper, and bring to a simmer, then cover and cook the meat until tender, about 45-60 minutes.
Dilute the peanut paste with some of the hot broth from the pot until smooth, then stir it back into the pot.

Add the carrots, cabbage, and sweet potato, and continue simmering on low heat, stirring occasionally to prevent the peanut sauce from sticking, until the vegetables are tender and the sauce has thickened, about 25-30 minutes.
Season with salt to taste.
Serve hot over steamed white rice.

title: Accara (Black-Eyed Pea Fritters)
instructions: Soak the black-eyed peas in water for several hours or overnight, then rub the beans between your hands or in a towel to loosen and remove the skins, rinsing away the hulls.
Drain the peeled beans and blend them with the chopped onion, scotch bonnet pepper, and garlic, adding only a small amount of water to form a thick, smooth batter.
Whip the batter vigorously with a spoon or whisk for several minutes to incorporate air, which helps the fritters become light and fluffy.
Season the batter with salt.
Heat the vegetable oil in a deep pot until hot, then drop spoonfuls of the batter into the oil.
Fry the fritters until golden brown and crisp on the outside, turning occasionally, about 4-5 minutes per batch.
Drain on paper towels and serve hot, plain or with a spicy pepper sauce.

title: Thiakry
ingredients: 2 cups couscous (millet couscous, thiakry grains) or fine dried millet couscous
instructions: Sprinkle the millet couscous grains with a little water and rub gently between your hands to moisten and separate them, breaking up any clumps.
Steam the moistened couscous in a covered pot or steamer basket over simmering water until the grains are tender and fully cooked, about 15-20 minutes, fluffing occasionally.
Let the cooked couscous cool completely, then transfer to a large bowl.
In a separate bowl, whisk together the yogurt, condensed milk, sugar, vanilla extract, and nutmeg until smooth.
Pour the yogurt mixture over the cooled couscous and stir gently to combine evenly.
Chill in the refrigerator for at least an hour before serving.
Serve cold as a dessert or snack.

title: Soupou Kandja
ingredients: 500g fish (smoked and fresh, mixed), cut into pieces
instructions: Heat the palm oil in a large pot and sauté the chopped onion until softened.
Add the chopped tomatoes and tomato paste, cooking until the mixture thickens into a sauce.
Add the water, whole scotch bonnet pepper, and both the smoked and fresh fish pieces, and bring to a simmer.
Stir in the chopped okra and continue to cook on medium heat, stirring frequently, until the okra breaks down and the soup becomes thick and slightly gelatinous, about 20-25 minutes.
Season with salt to taste, and simmer a few more minutes until the fish is fully cooked and flavors meld.
Serve hot over steamed white rice.

title: Ndambe
instructions: Soak the black-eyed peas for a couple of hours, then rinse and place in a pot with the water.
Bring to a boil and cook the beans until tender, about 40-45 minutes, adding water as needed.
In a separate pan, heat the palm oil and sauté the chopped onion until soft.
Add the chopped tomatoes, tomato paste, and whole scotch bonnet pepper, cooking until thickened into a sauce.
Stir the tomato sauce into the pot of cooked beans, mashing some of the beans lightly against the side of the pot to thicken the mixture.
Simmer together for 10-15 minutes, season with salt, and adjust consistency with reserved bean cooking liquid if needed.
Serve warm with slices of fresh baguette, a classic Senegalese street food breakfast.

title: Pastels
ingredients: 300g fresh fish fillet (such as tuna or mackerel), minced
instructions: Mix the flour and salt with water to form a smooth, firm dough, then knead briefly and let rest for 15-20 minutes covered with a damp cloth.
In a bowl, combine the minced fish, chopped onion, minced garlic, minced scotch bonnet pepper, parsley, and black pepper to make the filling, mixing well.
Roll out the dough thinly and cut into circles or small squares.
Place a spoonful of the fish filling onto each piece of dough, fold over into a half-moon or triangle shape, and press the edges firmly to seal, crimping with a fork if desired.
Heat the vegetable oil in a deep pot until hot.
Fry the pastels in batches until golden brown and crisp on both sides, about 4-6 minutes per batch.
Drain on paper towels and serve hot as a snack or appetizer.

title: Chebu Yapp
instructions: Heat the oil in a large pot and brown the beef chunks on all sides.
Add the chopped onions and sauté until softened, then stir in the chopped tomatoes and tomato paste, cooking until the mixture forms a thick red sauce.
Add water to cover, along with the bay leaf and whole scotch bonnet pepper, and simmer the beef until tender, about 45-60 minutes.
Add the cabbage, carrots, and eggplant to the pot and continue simmering until the vegetables are tender, then remove the meat and vegetables, reserving the broth.
Wash the rice and cook it in the reserved broth, adding it gradually and stirring occasionally, until the rice absorbs the broth and becomes tender and reddish in color.
Arrange the cooked rice on a large serving platter and top with the beef and vegetables.
Serve hot, often with a side of lime wedges and extra chili.

title: Caldou (Senegalese Fish and Vegetable Stew)
ingredients: 1 kg firm white fish (grouper or sea bream), cut into steaks
3 cups cooked white rice, for serving
instructions: Season the fish steaks with salt and half of the lime juice, and let marinate for 15 minutes.
Heat the vegetable oil in a large pot and sauté the chopped onion until softened.
Add the chopped tomatoes and cook until they break down into a light sauce.
Pour in the water, add the carrots, cassava, and whole scotch bonnet pepper, and simmer until the vegetables are nearly tender, about 15-20 minutes.
Add the marinated fish steaks to the pot and simmer gently until the fish is cooked through and the broth turns a pale golden color, about 10-15 minutes.
Stir in the remaining lime juice and adjust salt to taste.
Serve the fish and vegetables hot in their light broth over steamed white rice.

title: Egusi Soup
ingredients: 1 kg assorted meat and fish (beef, tripe, dried fish)
2 cups chopped spinach or pumpkin leaves (ugu)
instructions: Season the assorted meat and fish with onion, seasoning cubes, and salt, then boil until tender; reserve the stock
Heat the palm oil in a pot and fry the ground egusi, stirring continuously to form small lumps and cook off the raw taste
Add the blended pepper and chopped onion and fry for a few minutes
Pour in the reserved meat stock gradually, stirring to reach a thick, fluffy consistency
Add the boiled meat, fish, and ground crayfish, then simmer for 15 minutes
Stir in the chopped spinach or ugu leaves and cook for another 5 minutes
Adjust salt and seasoning, then serve hot with pounded yam, eba, or rice

title: Ogbono Soup
ingredients: 1 kg assorted meat and fish (beef, goat meat, dried fish)
instructions: Boil the assorted meat and fish with onion, seasoning cubes, and salt until tender, keeping the stock
Heat the palm oil in a separate pot and stir in the ground ogbono seeds, frying gently for a few minutes
Gradually pour in the meat stock while stirring continuously to draw out the characteristic drawy texture
Add the blended pepper, crayfish, and boiled meat and fish to the pot
Simmer on low heat for 15-20 minutes, stirring occasionally to prevent sticking
Stir in the chopped vegetables and cook for another 5 minutes
Season to taste and serve with pounded yam, garri, or fufu

title: Afang Soup
instructions: Season and boil the assorted meat, fish, and stockfish with onion, seasoning cubes, and salt until well cooked
In a pot, heat the palm oil and pour in the meat stock along with the boiled meat and fish
Add the ground crayfish and chili peppers, then simmer for about 10 minutes
Stir in the chopped waterleaf and cook for 5 minutes until it wilts and releases its water
Add the chopped afang leaves and stir well to combine
Simmer for another 8-10 minutes, stirring occasionally, until the soup thickens slightly
Season to taste and serve hot with eba, fufu, or pounded yam

title: Edikang Ikong
ingredients: 3 cups chopped ugu leaves (fluted pumpkin leaves)
1 kg assorted meat (beef, goat meat, tripe)
instructions: Season the assorted meat and fish with onion, seasoning cubes, and salt, then boil until tender, keeping the stock
Pour the palm oil into the pot with the meat stock and bring to a simmer
Add the ground crayfish and chili peppers, then stir in the boiled meat and fish
Add the chopped waterleaf first, allowing it to cook down for about 5 minutes
Stir in the chopped ugu leaves and combine thoroughly
Simmer for another 8 minutes until the vegetables are tender but still vibrant
Season with salt to taste and serve with pounded yam, fufu, or garri

title: Oha Soup
ingredients: 1 tbsp cocoyam paste or ede for thickening
instructions: Boil the cocoyam until soft, then pound or mash into a smooth paste for thickening the soup
Season and boil the assorted meat and dried fish with onion, seasoning cubes, and salt until tender
Heat the palm oil in a pot with the meat stock and stir in the mashed cocoyam paste to thicken
Add the boiled meat, fish, and ground crayfish, then simmer for 10 minutes
Gently stir in the sliced oha leaves, taking care not to overstir since oha leaves are delicate
Simmer for 3-5 minutes only, just until the leaves soften
Adjust seasoning and serve hot with pounded yam or fufu

title: Ewedu Soup
instructions: Boil the assorted meat and smoked fish with onion, seasoning cube, and salt until tender, reserving the stock
Cook the jute leaves in a separate pot with a little water until soft
Blend or grind the softened jute leaves briefly, then return to the pot
Add a small pinch of potash if desired and whisk vigorously to create the characteristic draw
Stir in the locust beans and the reserved meat stock with the boiled meat and fish
Simmer for 5 minutes, whisking occasionally
Serve hot alongside amala or eba

title: Okra Soup
ingredients: 1 cup chopped spinach or ugu leaves
1 kg assorted meat and fish (beef, dried fish)
instructions: Season and boil the assorted meat and fish with onion, seasoning cubes, and salt until tender, keeping the stock
Heat the palm oil in a pot and add the blended pepper, frying briefly
Pour in the reserved meat stock along with the boiled meat and fish
Add the diced okra and ground crayfish, stirring well
Simmer for 8-10 minutes until the okra softens and the soup slightly thickens
Stir in the chopped vegetables and cook for an additional 3 minutes
Season to taste and serve with garri, semovita, or pounded yam

title: Banga Soup
ingredients: 1 kg assorted meat and fish (beef, dried fish, smoked fish)
1 tbsp banga spice mix (or ground uziza and belebe leaves)
instructions: Extract palm fruit juice by boiling and pounding palm fruits, then sieve to obtain the thick banga extract
Season and boil the assorted meat and fish with onion, seasoning cubes, and salt until tender
Pour the palm fruit extract into a pot and bring to a boil, stirring occasionally
Add the boiled meat and fish along with their stock to the extract
Stir in the chili peppers and banga spice mix, then simmer for 20-25 minutes until the oil separates and rises to the top
Adjust seasoning and salt to taste
Serve hot with starch, garri, or fufu

title: Jollof Rice
instructions: Season the chicken with one chopped onion, a seasoning cube, and salt, then boil or grill until cooked; reserve the stock
Heat the oil in a large pot and fry the remaining chopped onion until fragrant
Add the blended tomatoes, tomato paste, and chili peppers, frying until the raw taste cooks off and the oil floats to the top
Stir in curry powder, thyme, remaining seasoning cube, and the reserved chicken stock
Add the washed parboiled rice, stirring to coat evenly in the sauce
Cover and cook on low heat until the rice is tender and the liquid is absorbed, stirring occasionally to prevent burning
Add the cooked chicken on top in the last few minutes to warm through
Fluff the rice and serve hot, garnished as desired

title: Coconut Rice
ingredients: 1 cup mixed vegetables (carrots, green peas, bell peppers)
instructions: Season the chicken with onion, a seasoning cube, and salt, then boil until tender; reserve the stock
In a pot, combine the coconut milk with the reserved chicken stock and bring to a simmer
Add curry powder, chili peppers, and the remaining seasoning cube
Stir in the washed parboiled rice, ensuring it is well submerged in the liquid
Cover and cook on low heat until the rice is tender and has absorbed the coconut milk, stirring occasionally
Add the mixed vegetables and cooked chicken in the last 10 minutes of cooking
Fluff the rice gently and serve warm

title: Fried Rice
ingredients: 3 cups parboiled rice, cooked and cooled
1 cup diced mixed vegetables (carrots, green beans, bell peppers)
instructions: Season and boil the chicken with a little onion, a seasoning cube, and salt until cooked; set aside
Boil the rice with a pinch of salt until just tender, then drain and cool to prevent clumping
Heat the oil in a large pan or wok and saute the chopped onion until translucent
Add the diced carrots, green beans, and peas, stir-frying for a few minutes
Add the shrimp and cooked chicken, stirring until the shrimp turns pink
Stir in curry powder and the remaining seasoning cube
Add the cooled rice and toss everything together until evenly coated and heated through
Adjust salt to taste and serve hot

title: Ofada Rice and Ayamase Sauce
instructions: Wash the ofada rice thoroughly and boil in plenty of water until tender, then drain and set aside
Season and boil the assorted meat and fish with onion, a seasoning cube, and salt until tender
Bleach the palm oil in a pot by heating it until it lightens in color, then allow it to cool slightly
Add the chopped onion to the bleached oil and fry briefly
Stir in the blended green peppers and chilies, frying until the raw taste cooks off
Add the locust beans, boiled meat and fish, and remaining seasoning cube, then simmer for 10-15 minutes
Adjust salt to taste and serve the ayamase sauce alongside the boiled ofada rice

title: Suya
ingredients: 2 tbsp suya spice mix (ground ginger, cayenne pepper, garlic powder, paprika)
instructions: Thread the thinly sliced beef onto wooden skewers
Mix the groundnut powder, suya spice mix, crushed seasoning cube, and salt together to make the yaji spice blend
Brush the skewered meat lightly with vegetable oil, then generously coat with the yaji spice blend
Grill the skewers over hot coals or under a grill, turning frequently, until the beef is cooked through and slightly charred
Brush with a little more oil halfway through grilling to keep the meat moist
Serve hot, garnished with sliced onions and extra spice mix on the side

title: Akara
ingredients: 2 cups black-eyed peas, soaked and peeled
instructions: Soak the black-eyed peas until softened, then rub off the skins and rinse thoroughly
Blend the peeled beans with the chopped onion and chili peppers, adding minimal water to form a thick, fluffy batter
Whisk the batter vigorously by hand to incorporate air until it becomes light and fluffy
Stir in the ground crayfish, seasoning cube, and salt
Heat the vegetable oil in a deep pot until hot
Scoop spoonfuls of the batter into the hot oil and fry until golden brown and cooked through, turning occasionally
Drain on paper towels and serve hot, often with bread or pap

title: Puff Puff
instructions: In a bowl, dissolve the yeast and a spoonful of sugar in warm water and let it sit for 5-10 minutes until frothy
In a large bowl, mix the flour, remaining sugar, salt, and nutmeg
Add the eggs and the yeast mixture to the dry ingredients, stirring to form a smooth, elastic batter
Cover the batter and let it rise in a warm place for about an hour until doubled and bubbly
Heat the vegetable oil in a deep pot until hot
Scoop small portions of the batter with wet hands and drop into the hot oil, frying until golden brown and cooked through
Drain on paper towels and serve warm, optionally dusted with sugar

title: Chin Chin
instructions: In a large bowl, combine the flour, milk powder, sugar, and nutmeg
Rub the butter into the dry mixture until it resembles coarse breadcrumbs
Add the eggs and mix, then gradually add water to form a firm, non-sticky dough
Knead the dough well, then roll it out flat on a floured surface
Cut the dough into small cubes or strips using a knife or chin chin cutter
Heat the vegetable oil in a deep pot and fry the dough pieces in batches until golden brown and crunchy
Drain on paper towels and allow to cool completely before storing in an airtight container

title: Moi Moi
ingredients: 2 cups black-eyed peas, soaked and peeled
1/4 cup vegetable oil or red palm oil
instructions: Soak the black-eyed peas, then rub off the skins and rinse thoroughly
Blend the peeled beans with the onion and chili peppers, adding a little water to form a smooth, thick batter
Stir in the vegetable oil, seasoning cube, and salt until well combined
Pour the batter into foil wraps, leaves, or small ramekins, adding a slice of boiled egg to each if desired
Cover and steam the wrapped batter in a pot of simmering water for 45 minutes to an hour, until firm and set
Check that a skewer inserted comes out clean to confirm it is fully cooked
Allow to cool slightly before unwrapping and serving

title: Kuli Kuli
instructions: Press the groundnut paste to release excess oil, kneading it repeatedly until it becomes firmer
